strings.「AI は鏡。江戸の絵を映すことはできるが、映すだけでは遊べない。」: 「AI は鏡。江戸の絵を映すことはできるが、映すだけでは遊べない。」 (“AI is a mirror. It can reflect Edo pictures, but you cannot play with a reflection alone.”)
strings.「…だからだろうか」という意味の、昔の言い方（精選版 日本国語大辞典より）。: An old way of saying “is it because …?” (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.「…でさえ」「…さえも」という意味の言葉です（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌では、: A word that means “even …” (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as “even a yakko”.
strings.「…なのだなあ」と、気がついて心を動かす気持ちをあらわす言い方です（精選版 日本: A phrase that shows the feeling of noticing something and being moved: “so it is …!” (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.「あさけ」という言葉は、夜明けのことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌の「朝気」: The word “asake” means dawn (from Digital Daijisen). The 朝気 in this poem may also mean around dawn, early in the morning, but both its reading and its meaning are not certain.
strings.「いさめのつづみ」とも言います。中国の伝説の王さまが、王に意見を言いたい人に打た: It is also called “isame no tsuzumi”. It is the drum that a legendary king of China is said to have put in front of his palace gate, so that people who wanted to tell the king their opinion could beat it (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「いやがる」は、いやだと思う心を、顔や態度に出すことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。: “Iyagaru” means to show in your face or manner that you dislike something (from Digital Daijisen). In the characters of the {0} transcription, it is written “iyakaru,” without the voicing mark.
strings.「うき」は、つらいこと、心がなやむことで、「憂し」という言葉から出ています（デジ: “Uki” means hardship, a troubled heart; it comes from the word “ushi” (painful) (from Digital Daijisen). The “uki toki wa” in this poem can be read as “in hard times”.
strings.「うき時は」の「時は（ときは）」には、「常盤（ときわ）」という人の名がかくしてあ: Arisaka writes that the “toki wa” in “uki toki wa” hides the name of a person, Tokiwa, and that this poem is about Tokiwa wandering in the village of Fushimi (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). In this poem, the meaning “in hard times” and Tokiwa’s name can be read as overlapping.
strings.「うなばら」と読みます。どこまでも広がっている、大きな海のことです（デジタル大辞: It is read “unabara”. It means a great sea that stretches as far as the eye can see (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「え」は、うしろに打ち消しの言葉が来ると、「…できない」という意味になります（デ: When “e” is followed by a negative word, it means “cannot …” (from Digital Daijisen). The “ete so oyobane” in this poem can also be read as “can never reach”, but the form with “te” in it is not certain.
strings.「おさな心」「おさな友だち」のように、「おさな」はほかの言葉の前に付いて、「おさ: As in “osana-gokoro” (a child’s heart) and “osana-tomodachi” (a childhood friend), “osana” goes in front of other words and adds the meaning “being young” or “when one was young” (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “osanagusa” in this poem can be read as “osana” with “kusa” added, but what “kusa” means is not certain.
strings.「おもいおもい（思い思い）」と読みます。「〳〵」は、前の言葉をもう一度くり返すし: It is read “omoi-omoi”. “〳〵” is a mark that means the word before it is repeated. It describes each person doing things the way they like (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「おもちゃを自分で作る体験は、科学で実験をすることと似ている。現象を個人的な体験: 「おもちゃを自分で作る体験は、科学で実験をすることと似ている。現象を個人的な体験とすることで喜びがあり、ひらめき、アタマを使い、科学が創られる」 (“Making a toy yourself is like doing an experiment in science. When a phenomenon becomes your own experience, there is joy; you get ideas, you use your head, and science is created.”)
strings.「かみ」は「紙」と「神」の両方に通じ、「出し」はお祭りの「山車（だし）」に掛けて: Arisaka writes that “kami” sounds like both “paper” and “god”, and that “dashi” is a play on the festival “dashi” (float) (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). This poem can be read as layering a story about paper and a story about a god’s festival in the same words.
strings.「きんとき」と読みます。坂田公時（金時）のことで、源頼光の家来の四天王の一人。子: It is read “Kintoki”. It means Sakata no Kintoki, one of the four great retainers (shitennō) of Minamoto no Yorimitsu (Raikō). His childhood name was Kintarō (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「くらいつく」は、かみつくことや、しっかりとりついてはなれないことです（デジタル: “Kuraitsuku” means to bite into something, or to cling tightly and not let go (from Digital Daijisen). “Nuru” shows that something has come about. Another word (for example “kurai,” rank) may also be played on, but this is not certain.
strings.「けもの」は、もとは「毛の物」という意味の言葉で、けだもののことです（デジタル大: “Kemono” originally meant “a thing with fur”, and it means a beast (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as saying “because it is a furry beast”.
strings.「げこ」と読みます。お酒が飲めない人、お酒が好きでない人のことです（デジタル大辞: It is read “geko”. A person who cannot drink sake, or who does not like sake (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「こそ」は、ある言葉を取りあげて、強く言うための言葉です。昔の言葉では、「こそ」: “Koso” is a word that picks out another word to say it strongly. In old Japanese, when “koso” is used, the form of the word at the end of the sentence changes (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read that “iru” (ゐる, to be) has become “ire” (ゐれ).
strings.「こぞう（小僧）」と読みます。年の小さい男の子のことです（精選版 日本国語大辞典: It is read “kozō”. It means a young boy (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). Here it refers to the naked boy doll in the picture.
strings.「こと（琴）」は日本の楽器の名前で、江戸時代からは、とくに箏（そう）を指して言い: “Koto” is the name of a Japanese instrument; since the Edo period it has meant especially the sō (a long zither) (from Digital Daijisen). The “koto” in this poem can be read as layering the koto of the board koto in the picture and the “koto” of “… suru koto mo” (even doing …), but that is not certain.
strings.「こま」と読みます。ここでは絵の中の花の形をした玩具のことで、ふつう「花独楽」と: It is read “koma” (top). Here it means the flower-shaped toy in the picture. It was usually called “hana-goma” (flower top) and is said to have been a toy for small children (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「こま」は独楽のことで、また「高麗（こま）」にも通じていて、次の「もろこし」につ: Arisaka writes that “koma” means a top, and that it also sounds like “Koma” (高麗, an old name for a kingdom in Korea), which links it to the next word, “Morokoshi” (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「ころぶ」は、体がたおれることをいいます（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌の「ころひ: “Korobu” means that your body falls over (from Digital Daijisen). The “korohishitsu” in this poem means “korobishitsu” and can be read as “fell down”.
strings.「ございます」と同じ意味の言葉「ごわる」の形です。江戸時代に、おもに奴が使った言: A form of “gowaru”, a word that means the same as “gozaimasu” (a polite way to say “there is” or “it is”). In the Edo period, it was mostly yakko who spoke this way (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.「さかけ」と読みます。お酒のにおいや、お酒を飲んで酔っている様子のことです（デジ: It is read “sakake”. It means the smell of sake, or being drunk from drinking sake (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「しょうぞく」と読みます。身につける衣服のことで、とくに晴れの場のために整えた着: It is read “shōzoku”. It means clothes that are worn, especially garments prepared for a special occasion (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「じっとしていない」という意味に、動物の「犬」を掛けたものだろう、と有坂は書いて: Arisaka writes that it is probably “jitto shite inu” (does not keep still) with a play on “inu” (dog) (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「じゃ」は大きなへびのことで、富士権現のおみやげに売られた麦わらのへびも、そう呼: “Ja” means a big snake; the wheat-straw snakes sold as souvenirs of Fuji Gongen are also called that (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “jiya” in this poem can be read as the “ja” of “uchiwa ja” (it is a fan) with a play on this snake.
strings.「じゃれる」は、まとわりついたり、ふざけたりして遊ぶことです（デジタル大辞泉より: “Jareru” means to play by clinging to something or fooling around (from Digital Daijisen). The “jiyare-jiyare shi” in this poem can be read as playing over and over: frolicking, and frolicking again.
strings.「そのまま」と読みます。「ゝ」は、前の字をもう一度くり返すしるしです。「そのまま: Read as “sonomama.” “ゝ” is a mark that repeats the character before it. “Sonomama” can mean “exactly as it is” (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as “just like the real thing.”
strings.「その頃その頃」という言葉の中に、絵の玩具「芋虫ころころ」の「ころころ」が入って: The words “sono koro sono koro” (each in its own season) contain the “koro-koro” of “Imomushi Koro-koro” (rolling caterpillar), a toy in the picture (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「たがわない（まちがえない）」という意味です。終わりの「ざる」で、絵の玩具「猿の: It means “tagawanai” (does not get it wrong). The ending “zaru” is a play on the monkey (saru) of “Saru no Ki-nobori” (monkey climbing a tree), a toy in the picture (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「たぐい」のこと。同じくらいの物、ならぶ物という意味です（デジタル大辞泉より）。: It means “tagui”: something of the same level, something that is its equal (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「たぶらかす」のことで、人をだまして、まよわせることです（デジタル大辞泉より）。: It means “taburakasu”: to trick people and lead them astray (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「ちいちい」はねずみのことで、この歌の福の神は大黒天（大黒さま）だ、と有坂は書い: Arisaka writes that “chii-chii” means a rat (nezumi), and that the god of fortune in this poem is Daikokuten (Daikoku) (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「つく（搗く）」は、麦や米などの穀物を、杵や棒の先で強くたたいて、からを取ったり: “Tsuku” (搗く) means to strike grain such as barley or rice hard with a pestle or the end of a stick, to take off the husks or to crush it (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「てっぺん」のこと。いちばん上、いちばんすぐれている物、という意味です（精選版: It means “teppen”: the very top, or the very best thing (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.「とうとう」は、ついに、結局、という意味の言葉です。また、「どうどう」は、馬や牛: “Tōtō” is a word meaning at last, in the end. Also, “dōdō” is the call used to stop a horse or a cow (from Digital Daijisen). The “tō-tō” in this poem can be read as either one, but that is not certain.
strings.「どうぜん」と読み、「同然」と同じ。…と変わらない、…と同じことだ、という意味で: It is read “dōzen” and is the same as 同然 (dōzen). It means “no different from …” or “the same as …” (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「どきつく」と読みます。有坂は、胸がどきどきする様子を表す言葉と読み、そう取れば: It is read “dokitsuku”. Arisaka reads it as a word for the heart pounding, and writes that, taken this way, the first half of the poem more or less makes sense (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「なくね」と読みます。「ね」は声のことで、人の泣き声にも、鳥などの鳴き声にも使い: It is read “nakune”. “Ne” means a voice or sound, and it is used both for a person crying and for the calls of birds and other animals (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「ぬらん」は、「きっと…してしまったのだろう」と、もう起きたことを思いうかべる言: “Nuran” is a way of imagining something that has already happened: “surely it must have …” (from Digital Daijisen). So “suzu ya idenuran” becomes “has a bell come out?”
strings.「のぼり（幟）」は、五月の端午の節句に立てて飾る旗のことでもあります（デジタル大: “Nobori” is also the name of the banners put up for the Boys’ Festival (Tango no Sekku) in the fifth month (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as layering “noboru” (to climb) bamboo and this “nobori” (banner).
strings.「のぼり（幟）」は、鯉のぼりや五月幟のように、五月の端午の節句にかざる物のことも: “Nobori” (banner) also means things put up for the Boys’ Festival (Tango no Sekku) in the fifth month, such as carp streamers and May banners (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as a joyful May banner (whether other words are layered in is not certain).
strings.「のろま」と読みます。動きがにぶいという意味の「のろま」と、「のろま人形」を掛け: It is read “noroma”. It plays on “noroma”, meaning slow and dull, and the “noroma puppet”. The noroma puppet is a puppet that a man named Noromatsu Kanbei began to use in Izumi-dayū’s plays, and the usual explanation is that “noroma” is a shortened form of his name (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「はじめから組み立てる」を押すと、{0} 手目から組み立てます。「次へ」で {1: Press “はじめから組み立てる” (Assemble from the start) to assemble it from step {0}. Then press “次へ” (Next) to go {1} step at a time.
strings.「はじめる」を押すと、ブラウザ（ネットを見るアプリ）が声を字にします。そのとき、: When you press “Start,” the browser (the app you use to look at the web) turns your voice into text. Your voice may be sent to the company that makes the browser when this happens. This page only listens for the words that move the steps along. It does not keep your voice or the text.

When you press “Start,” the browser (the app you use to look at the web) turns your voice into text. Your voice may be sent to the company that makes the browser when this happens. This page only listens for the words that move the steps along. It does not keep your voice or the text. This is a prototype. We are trying out a way to view it on an HMD (a screen worn on the head), so both hands stay free.
strings.「はづす（外す）」は、取りはなすことで、取りつけてある物や、かけてある物に使いま: “Hazusu” (to take off) means to remove something, and is used for things that are attached or hung (from Digital Daijisen). The “hazuseshi” in this poem can be read as “took down”.
strings.「ひとつである」という意味の言葉に、鈴を掛けたものだそうです。それでも、歌全体の: It is said to be a phrase meaning “being one”, with a play on the bell (suzu). Even so, Arisaka writes that the meaning of the whole poem cannot be made clear (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「ふたつの頭」。絵の二つの首人形のことで、あやつり人形から生まれた人形だそうです: “Two heads”. These are the two head puppets in the picture, which are said to have grown out of theater puppets (ayatsuri ningyō) (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「まい」は、「…しないだろう」とおしはかる気持ちや、「…しないつもりだ」という気: “Mai” is a word that expresses a guess that something will not happen, or an intention not to do something; attached to “suru” (to do), it can become “sumai” (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “kachi mo sumai” in this poem can be read as “will not win either”.
strings.「まいる」には、負ける・降参する、という意味があります（精選版 日本国語大辞典よ: “Mairu” can mean to lose or to give up (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). Here it seems to read as “never loses”, but whether that is really the meaning is not known.
strings.「まことと や 見ん」と読みます。「まこと」は、本当のこと、うそでないことです（: It is read “makoto to ya min”. “Makoto” means the truth, something that is not a lie (from Digital Daijisen). It is a way of saying “would one take it to be real?”
strings.「めでたい」は、うれしくて、お祝いするのにふさわしいようすを言います（デジタル大: “Medetai” describes something happy and worth celebrating (from Digital Daijisen). The “metetaki” in this poem means “medetaki” and can be read as “joyful”.
strings.「めでたくかしく」は、相手をほめて、うやまう気持ちをこめ、女の人が手紙のおしまい: “Medetaku kashiku” is a phrase that women wrote at the end of a letter, praising the reader and showing respect; it is also said “medetaku kashiko” (from Digital Daijisen). Whether the “medetaku kashiko” in this poem is the same phrase is not certain.
strings.「もとより」は、はじめから、もともと、という意味です（デジタル大辞泉より）。この: “Moto yori” means from the start, originally (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as saying that paper (kami, also “god”) has always been mixed in with the dust.
strings.「もののふ」は、主君（つかえる殿さま）のために、戦いに出る人のことです（デジタル: “Mononofu” means a person who goes out to fight for their lord (the ruler they serve) (from Digital Daijisen). If 武士 in this poem is read “mononofu”, it has five sounds and fits the form of the poem, but the characters of its furigana (the small reading letters) are not certain.
strings.「もろこしが原」がどこかはわからないが、昔、大山のふもとの海べのあたりをそう呼ん: Arisaka writes that he does not know where “Morokoshi ga hara” is, but that it seems to come from a name once used for the seashore area at the foot of Ōyama (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). The exact place is not known.
strings.「やっこ」のこと。江戸時代に武家に仕えた人で、行列の先頭に立って、槍などを持って: It means “yakko”: in the Edo period, a servant of a samurai household, who walked at the front of a procession carrying a spear or the like (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「やつし」は歌舞伎の役柄の言葉です。有坂は「やつしの色事師」を、遊ぶことの好きな: “Yatsushi” is a kabuki word for a type of role. Arisaka reads “yatsushi no irogotoshi” as a handsome man who loves to have fun (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「やど」は「宿」とも「屋戸」とも書き、家やすみかのことです（デジタル大辞泉より）: “Yado” is written either 宿 or 屋戸, and means a house or a home (from Digital Daijisen). The “yato” (や戸) in this poem can be read as this “yado”, but that is not certain.
strings.「よく似（に）た」と「にわとり（鶏）」を掛けた言い方です。「よく似」の「に」が、: A play on “yoku nita” (looks very much like) and “niwatori” (chicken). The “ni” of “yoku ni(ta)” is also the “ni” of “niwatori” (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「よしとも」は源義朝の名で、「よい友」にも聞こえるようにしてある、と有坂は書いて: Arisaka writes that “Yoshitomo” is the name of Minamoto no Yoshitomo, made so that it can also be heard as “yoi tomo” (a good friend) (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). The “yoshitomo mo naki” in this poem can be read two ways: “there is no good friend” and “Yoshitomo is not here”.
strings.「わんわん」と読みます。「〳〵」は、前の言葉をもう一度くり返すしるしです。犬の鳴: It is read “wanwan”. “〳〵” is a mark that means the word before it is repeated. From the sound a dog makes, small children call a dog this, like “bow-wow” (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.「下がる」には、高い所から低い所へ移る、という意味があります（デジタル大辞泉より: “Sagaru” means to move from a high place to a low place (from Digital Daijisen). The “sagarishi” in this poem can be read as a kite that came down from the sky. How to read 下 is not certain.
strings.「世にたぐいあらじ（世の中にならぶものがない）」と「あら人神」の二つを、一つにつ: A phrase that joins two things into one: “yo ni tagui araji” (there is nothing equal to it in the world) and “arahitogami” (a god who appears in this world) (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「今日（きょう）」のことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌では、昔のかなづかいで: It means “kyō” (today) (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as written “kefu” in the old way of spelling with kana.
strings.「伊勢のようだ」ということ。芝神明は伊勢の神宮ゆかりの物をまつり、もとの土地も伊: It means “like Ise”. Arisaka writes that the poem says this because Shiba Shinmei enshrines things connected with the Ise Shrine, and its original site was also said to be connected with the Ise Shrine (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「伏見街道」は、京都の五条から南へ下って、伏見まで続く道の呼び名です（デジタル大: “Fushimi Kaidō” is the name of the road that runs south from Gojō in Kyoto down to Fushimi (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as tying the “Fushimi” of Fushimi dolls and the road walked while thinking of one’s child to this road.
strings.「作り物」。本物に似せて、人が手で作った物のことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。: “Tsukurimono” (a made thing): something people make by hand to look like the real thing (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.「入相の鐘」は、夕方にお寺でつく鐘の音や、その鐘のことです（デジタル大辞泉より）: “Iriai no kane” is the sound of the bell rung at a temple in the evening, or that bell (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as the evening bell of the mountain temple.

strings.「型紙の版」は玩具ごとの型紙の組の番号で、紙の題にも刷ります。「エンジンの版」は: The “template version” is the number given to each toy’s set of templates; it is also printed in the title on the sheet. The “engine version” is the number in the ledger of the engine that produces the templates.
strings.「塵にまじわる」は、世の中の人たちと分けへだてなくまじって暮らす、という意味の言: “Chiri ni majiwaru” (to mix with the dust) is a phrase that means to live among the people of the world without setting yourself apart (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “chiri ni mashiharu” in this poem is this phrase, and it can be read as layering two ideas: paper that has always been in the dust, and a god who mixes into the human world.
strings.「届かない」という意味の「及ばぬ」に、羽根つき遊びの「追羽根」を掛けた言葉だそう: It is said to join “oyobanu” (cannot reach) with “oibane”, the shuttlecock game played with battledores (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). In this poem, it can be read as using words from the shuttlecock game for the feeling of not being able to reach the one you love.
strings.「山伏（やまぶし）」のこと。山伏は、山にこもって修行をする人です（デジタル大辞泉: It means “yamabushi” (mountain monk). A yamabushi is a person who stays in the mountains to train in religious practice (from Digital Daijisen). Why “yama” (mountain) is written twice is not known.
strings.「工夫」は、あれこれ考えをめぐらして、よいやり方を見つけ出すことで、そのやり方の: “Kufū” means thinking hard to find a good way to do something, or that way itself (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as the way the teahouse thought of to keep its customers coming.
strings.「心棒」は、こまや車輪のように回る物の、まん中にある棒のことです（デジタル大辞泉: “Shinbō” (心棒) is the pole in the middle of something that spins, such as a top or a wheel (from Digital Daijisen). The “koma mo shinbō” in this poem can be read as a pun that layers the same-sounding “shinbō” (patience) and “shinbō” (center pole), saying that a top (koma) needs its “shinbō” too.
strings.「怠る」は、やるべきことをやらずにいる、なまける、という意味です（デジタル大辞泉: “Okotaru” means not to do what you should do; to slack off (from Digital Daijisen). The “okotare ha” in this poem means “okotareba” and can be read as “if you slack off”.
strings.「木をかえて」のことで、野の猿が、五月の端午の節句には木を替えて竹にのぼる、とい: It means “ki o kaete” (changing trees). Arisaka writes that it is enough to take it to mean roughly that a wild monkey changes trees and climbs bamboo at the Boys’ Festival (Tango no Sekku) in the fifth month (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). It can also be read as a play on “ki o kaete” (changing one’s mood), but that is not certain.
strings.「果ては」は、さいごには、とうとう、という意味です（精選版 日本国語大辞典より）: “Hate wa” means in the end, at last (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). In this poem, it can be read as “at the end of playing and frolicking”.
strings.「汲めや汲め」。さあ汲め、汲め、という呼びかけです。「和泉」の「泉」の水を汲むこ: “Kume ya kume”: a call meaning “Come on, pour, pour!” It plays on drawing water from the “izumi” (spring) in the name Izumi, and pouring sake (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.「湯殿」は、山形県にある出羽三山の一つ、湯殿山を短くして言う時にも使いますが、も: “Yudono” is also used as a short name for Mount Yudono, one of the Three Mountains of Dewa in Yamagata Prefecture, but its original meaning is a bathroom (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “Yudono” in this poem can be read as Mount Yudono (whether it also layers the meaning of a bathroom is not certain).
strings.「満尾」は、物語などが終わりまでできあがることで、もとは連歌や連句をひと巻き終え: “Manbi” means that a story or the like is completed to the end; originally it meant finishing one full round of renga or renku (linked verse) (from Digital Daijisen). The “manbi itashite” in this poem can be read as saying that this picture book ends with this picture.
strings.「猛し」は、強くて勇ましいようすを表す言葉です（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌の「: “Takeshi” is a word for being strong and brave (from Digital Daijisen). The “takeki kemono” in this poem can be read as a strong, brave beast, that is, the lion of Shakkyō.
strings.「獅子に牡丹」は、どっしりした獅子と、はなやかな牡丹の花とを組み合わせた絵柄で、: “Shishi ni botan” (a lion with peonies) is a design that puts together a powerful lion and showy peony flowers, and it is also used to mean a pair that goes well together (from Digital Daijisen). The “hotan” in this poem means “botan” (peony), and can be read as a word that comes from this pairing.
strings.「白いのは源氏」。源氏は、平家の赤い旗に対して、白い旗をしるしにしました（精選版: “The white one is the Genji.” Against the red flags of the Heike, the Genji used white flags as their sign (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).

strings.「示し」は、お手本となって教えること、またはその教えのことです（デジタル大辞泉よ: “Shimeshi” means teaching by being an example, or that teaching (from Digital Daijisen). The “shi no shimeshi” in this poem can be read as the teaching that a master (a teacher) gives his pupil.
strings.「科学の面白さを伝える。自然とのコールアンドレスポンス。おもちゃで遊び続ける。」: 「科学の面白さを伝える。自然とのコールアンドレスポンス。おもちゃで遊び続ける。」 (“Share how fun science is. Call and response with nature. Keep playing with toys.”)
strings.「穂に出づ」は、外にあらわれて、人に気づかれるようになることです（デジタル大辞泉: “Ho ni izu” (to come out in ears, like grain) means to show on the outside and be noticed by people (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as the hidden feeling coming out into the open, but whether “nu” means “has …” or “does not …” is not certain.

strings.「竹馬」は、子どもの遊び道具で、竹で作って馬に見立てた物です（精選版 日本国語大: “Takeuma” is a child’s plaything, made of bamboo to look like a horse (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). In this poem, it can be read as something that brings back memories of childhood play.

strings.「若子（わこ）」は、身分の高い家の男の子のことで、男の子を親しんで呼ぶ言い方でも: “Wako” means a boy of a high-ranking family, and it is also a friendly way to speak of a boy (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as the boy who will carry on the family.

strings.いさめの太鼓にはこけが深く生えて、鳥もおどろかない。けれども、この細工には、みん: The remonstrance drum is deep in moss, and even the birds are not startled. But at this craftwork, everyone is startled (“this craftwork” follows the character 此 in Arisaka’s {0} book).

strings.うぐいすは春、いもむしは秋のものだからだろうか。どちらも、その頃その頃の時をまち: Is it because the bush warbler belongs to spring and the caterpillar to autumn? Neither of them mistakes its time, each in its own season.
strings.うちわを売り歩く人のこと。江戸時代、夏のはじめになると、うちわをたくさん持って町: A person who walked around selling round fans (uchiwa). In the Edo period, at the start of summer, they went around town carrying many fans (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.うちわ売りに姿を変えた色男。ある時はまた、頬かぶりの姿になる。: A handsome lover disguised as a fan seller. At other times, he wears a hōkaburi (a cloth wrapped over the head and cheeks).
strings.うっかりして、体にきずを受けることや、そのきずのことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。: Getting a wound on your body by accident, or that wound (from Digital Daijisen). The “kega naku” in this poem can be read as “fell, but was not hurt”.

utsushi is one concrete example of using the paper to toy engine to make Edo toys from paper and try them out (Edo toys are the first subject; the engine’s way of laying out parts, its checks, its {0}D checks, and its improvement loop do not depend on the subject).

strings.うつしは、みんなが使えるサービスとして作りました。学校の理科の授業や研究、博物館: utsushi was made as a service anyone can use. It started with education in mind: school science classes, research, and museums. The way of seeing behind it belongs to the creator of this site alone, but the experience itself, making something from paper and checking it, is something we hope everyone will try.
strings.うつしは、学校や博物館などで使える、ワークショップを支えるサービスです。: utsushi is a service that supports workshops in schools, museums and other places.
strings.うつしも、江戸の絵本に残る絵と歌と向き合い、失われた動きを紙で解釈し直します。: utsushi, too, faces the pictures and poems left in an Edo picture book, and reinterprets the lost movements in paper.
strings.うまくいかなくても、直して、もう一度刷れば、すぐに作り直せます。: Even if it does not go well, you can fix it, print it again, and remake it right away.
strings.うれしさを言い表した言葉で、そこに疱瘡よけの木菟（みみずく）を結び付けた、と有坂: Arisaka reads it as a word that expresses joy, to which the poem ties the eared owl (mimizuku), a charm against smallpox (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). In this poem, it can be read as layering “tsukuzuku” (deeply) and the “zuku” of the owl in the picture.

strings.おもちゃのことで、手に持って遊ぶ物や、その遊びをいいます（デジタル大辞泉より）。: A toy: something you hold in your hands to play with, or that kind of play (from Digital Daijisen). The “teasohi no uma” in this poem can be read as a toy horse.
strings.おもちゃの大きさ（寸法）を入れると、エンジンが、紙で作るための型紙（切って、折っ: When you enter a toy’s size (its dimensions), the engine produces a template for making it from paper (a drawing to cut out, fold, and glue).
strings.お祭りのときに、人形や花をかざって、引いて町を歩く屋台を「山車（だし）」と言いま: A float decorated with dolls or flowers that is pulled through town at a festival is called a “dashi” (from Digital Daijisen). The “dashi” in this poem can be read two ways: as “dasu” (to bring out) and as this float.
strings.お祭りを見物するとき、牛車を止める場所をめぐって、お供の人どうしが争うことです。: A quarrel between the servants of different people over where to stop their ox-drawn carriages while watching a festival. The best-known example is the Kamo Festival scene in The Tale of Genji, where the servants of Rokujō no Miyasudokoro and of Aoi no Ue fought (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.お金がたくさんあって、位も高いことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌では、人形屋: Having a lot of money and a high rank (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as the doll seller becoming rich and doing well.
strings.からくりの「ちかふ」も見えて（「ちかふ」が何かは、わかっていません）、奴でさえ、: The karakuri’s “chikafu” can be seen too (what “chikafu” is, is not known), and even a yakko, once he grows old and weak, is turned around by sake (“turn” links to the top in the picture).
strings.けれど、作って確かめる体験は、だれにでもできます。同じ型紙から作っても、つまずく: But anyone can have the experience of making something and checking it. Even with the same template, each person gets stuck in different places and notices different things.
strings.ここの弓矢は、絵にある飾りの弓矢のことで、いわゆる「破魔弓（はまゆみ）」だ、と有: Arisaka writes that the bow and arrows here are the decorative bow and arrows in the picture, the kind called “hamayumi” (a bow to drive away evil) (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). This poem can be read as setting the boy and the bow and arrows side by side as the two treasures of a samurai house.

strings.この言葉には、別の意味もこめられています。「ましら」は猿のことです。別の意味が何: These words also carry another meaning. “Mashira” means monkey. What the other meaning is, is not known (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.これがあの、いつも「まいった」と言わない与次郎兵衛か。つり合いものの中の、いちば: So this is the famous Yojirobē, who never says “I give up”! The very best of all balancing toys. The meaning of “mairanu” is not clearly known.
strings.さあ、お酒を汲め、汲め。和泉太夫が語る公時も、お酒が入っていなければ、のろま（の: Come now, pour, pour the sake! Even the Kintoki that Izumi-dayū tells of is just a noroma (a slowpoke, like the noroma puppet) if there is no sake in him.
strings.じゃれて、じゃれて、しまいには湯殿（湯殿山）の大おどり。松坂をこえて、鹿島踊がは: Playing and frolicking, until in the end it is the great dance of Yudono (Mount Yudono). Crossing Matsuzaka, the Kashima dance begins. The poem does not say who is playing with what.
strings.ずっと前の時のこと。昔にあったできごとのことも言います（精選版 日本国語大辞典よ: A time long ago. It also means things that happened in the past (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).

strings.ちいちい（ねずみ）に乗ってやって来る、車の福の神（大黒さま）。きのえねの年の、縁: Riding on a chii-chii (a rat), here comes the god of fortune (Daikoku) on his cart, from the lucky direction in a year of kinoene. “Notte kuruma” can be read as layering “notte kuru” (comes riding) and “kuruma” (cart).

strings.つけで売った品物のお金を集めて回る人や、そのお金を集めること。「かけごい」とも読: A person who goes around collecting money for goods sold on credit, or the collecting itself. It is also read “kakegoi” (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.つらい時は、よい友もいない（義朝もいない）。夜の鶴が子を思って鳴くように、子を思: In hard times, there is no good friend (and no Yoshitomo). Like a crane crying at night for its young, the road walked while thinking of one’s child is the Fushimi Kaidō. Arisaka Yotarō reads “toki wa” as hiding the name of Tokiwa Gozen (the mother of Ushiwaka).
strings.どう工夫したかあとで教えてください。写真や動画でもいいです。: Tell us later what you changed. Photos or videos are fine too.
strings.なまけると転ぶよ、と師匠が弟子に教える。人も「しんぼう」（がまん）が大事、こまも: “If you slack off, you will fall over,” the teacher tells his pupil. People need “shinbō” (patience), and tops need “shinbō” (a center pole) too.
strings.のちに「やじろべえ」と呼ばれる玩具の、もとになった人形です。与次郎と呼ばれた人が: The doll that the toy later called “yajirobē” (a balancing toy) came from. It is said that the name comes from a man called Yojirō, who performed with this doll (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.はっきりしない、どちらとも決まらない様子（精選版 日本国語大辞典より）。: Unclear; not settled either way (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.ひな人形は紙、小僧ははだか、こまは布。それぞれ思い思いの姿が、おもしろい。: The hina doll is paper, the little boy is naked, and the top is cloth. Each has a look all its own, and that is fun to see.
strings.ひな人形は紙でできている、ということ。紙のひな人形は「立雛」とも呼ばれ、座った形: It means that the hina doll is made of paper. Paper hina dolls are also called “tachibina” (standing hina dolls), and they are said to be a much older form than hina dolls that sit (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.ぴいぴいも、ぶうぶうも、笛のなかまの玩具の名前です（有坂与太郎『日本玩具史 後編: Both “pii-pii” and “bū-bū” are names of toys in the whistle family (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). This poem lays the names of the two toys over the sound of crying and the sound of grumbling.
strings.ぶつぶつと文句や小言を言うこと（精選版 日本国語大辞典より）。: Muttering complaints and grumbles (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).

strings.もともと塵にまじわる紙（神）なので、お祭りのたびに張りぬいて出す（山車）。めでた: Since it is paper (kami, which also means “god”) that has always mixed with the dust, at every festival it is made into papier-mâché and brought out (dashi, which also means a festival float). “Medetaku, kashiko.” Why “medetaku kashiko” is attached to the end of the poem is not known.
strings.ものごとが順を追って進んだり、ようすが少しずつ変わったりするのを表す言葉で、「だ: A word for things going forward step by step, or changing little by little; it means “gradually” (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). “〳〵” is a mark that repeats the two characters before it, so here it can be read as “shidai shidai”.
strings.ものの値段や代金のことで、「あたい」とも、それが変わった形の「あたえ」とも言いま: The price or cost of something; it is said “atai”, or “atae”, a changed form of it (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). In this poem, it can be read as the price of the toy horse.

strings.エンジンは「部品を並べる → 刷る前に確かめる（はみ出し・重なり・ちゃんと動くか: The engine works in this order: lay out the parts → check before printing (parts sticking out, overlaps, and a calculation of whether it will move) → print → read the printed sheet back and check it.

strings.一本の糸。後に出てくる「御縁」の言葉へつなぐための、前置きになっています（有坂与: A single thread. It is a lead-in that sets up the word “goen” (a bond between people), which comes later (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.一本の糸をご縁のきっかけにして、袖を引いてみたいなあ。絵の中の若衆のすがたに。: With a single thread as the start of a bond, how I would love to tug at a sleeve: the sleeve of the wakashu (young man) in the picture.
strings.七福神のように、人に幸せをさずけてくれると考えられてきた神さまのことです（デジタ: A god who has long been thought to bring people happiness, like the Seven Gods of Good Fortune (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as Daikoku, who comes riding a rat.
strings.下がってきた凧（たこ）を、海のたこのように焼いて食べようと思ったけれど、袖凧も鳶: I thought I would grill and eat the kite (tako) that came down, like an octopus (also tako) from the sea, but the sleeve kite and the tobi kite were both paper (“kaminari” can be read as a play on the thunder kite in the picture).
strings.世にたぐひあら人神: 世にたぐひあら人神 (yo ni taguhi arahitogami)
strings.世の中にならぶものがない、この世に姿を現した神さまの昔のお話を、五つや三つの子ど: Children of five or three, listen well to the old story of the god who has no equal in the world and who appeared in this world. Which god it is, and what the story is, is not known.
strings.中国の白居易の詩から出た「夜の鶴」は、親が子をかわいく思う気持ちの深さをたとえて: “Yoru no tsuru” (the crane at night), which comes from a poem by Bai Juyi of China, is a phrase that stands for how deeply parents love their children (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, Tokiwa’s love for her children can be read as being compared to the crane at night.
strings.丸い井戸のまわりを囲む、わくのこと。『伊勢物語』の歌から、幼なじみという意味にも: The frame that goes around a round well. Because of a poem in The Tales of Ise (Ise Monogatari), it is also used to mean a childhood friend (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.予算の累計の停止線に達しました。日が変わっても聞けません: The total budget stop line has been reached. You cannot ask even after the day changes
strings.五歳や三歳の、小さい子どものことと読めます。有坂は、「いにしえを」に続くこの「五: It can be read as small children of five or three years old. Arisaka thinks that this “itsutsu” (five), which follows “inishie o”, must hide the phrase “mukashi o ima ni” (the past, brought back to now), but he says he cannot grasp the meaning of the poem as a whole (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).

strings.人の前に姿を現して、ふしぎな力を見せる神さまのこと。住吉の神や北野の天神さまを、: A god who appears before people and shows wondrous powers. The god of Sumiyoshi and the Tenjin god of Kitano were often called this (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).

strings.今の「そそう（粗相）」は、そそっかしいことや、よく確かめずにふるまってしまうこと: Today’s “sosō” (粗相) means being careless, or acting without checking well (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “sosō” in this poem can be read with that meaning. The furigana characters are not certain.

strings.今日はもう、笹湯（病気が治った子にかけるお湯）もすませた。そのうれしさを、家じゅ: Today the sasayu (the hot water poured over a child who has gotten well) is already done. The whole household feels that joy deeply, “tsukuzuku” (with “zuku-zuku” a play on mimizuku, the eared owl). What “tsutsumamori” refers to is not known.
strings.仏さまの教えを守る四人の神。そこから、ある集まりの中でいちばんすぐれた四人のこと: Four gods who guard the teachings of the Buddha. From this, it also means the four best people in a gathering (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.仏さまを心から信じる気持ちを表す言葉。仏さまの名前を呼ぶ時に、前に付けます（デジ: A word that expresses heartfelt faith in a Buddha. It is said before a Buddha’s name when calling it (from Digital Daijisen).

strings.伊勢のやうだ: 伊勢のやうだ (Ise no yau da)
strings.伊勢（今の三重県伊勢市）の海辺に、夫婦岩で知られる「二見浦（ふたみがうら）」があ: On the coast of Ise (now Ise City in Mie Prefecture) there is “Futamigaura”, known for the Meoto Iwa (Wedded Rocks) (from Digital Daijisen). Whether the “futami” in this poem refers to it is not known.
strings.伝えたい事があっても、相手の年齢も、場所も、用意できる物や予算も、さまざまです。: Even when you have something to share, the age of the people you want to reach, the place, and what you can prepare or afford all vary. With paper, scissors, and glue, you can share many things. That is the basic idea behind utsushi.
strings.作った人の報告やワークショップの感想から直しの案が生まれ、人が選んだ案で直すと、: Makers’ reports and workshop feedback lead to proposed fixes. When a fix that people chose is made, the template version and the engine version go up.
strings.作った人の報告・ワークショップの感想・ワークショップの型紙レビュー: Makers’ reports, workshop feedback, workshop template reviews
strings.作った人の記録を AI（Claude）が読んで、動かなかった原因を考える事もあり: The AI (Claude) sometimes reads makers’ records and thinks about why something did not move. Until a person checks that reading, it stays a proposal and is not used to fix the template.
strings.作りながら見る（試作） 仮説の紙・版 {0}: Make while you watch (untested draft) · Guess sheet · version {0}

strings.写しは、ただまねる事ではありません。昔の名人や名品と向き合い、その心をくみ取って: Utsushi is not simple copying. It means facing the masters and masterpieces of the past, taking in their spirit, and making the work anew with your own hands (as in the tea ceremony, Japanese painting, ceramics, lacquer, Noh, Kabuki, and honkadori in waka poetry).
strings.凧あげの時に子どもが歌ったはやし歌に、凧（たこ）を海の「たこ」に掛けて、下がって: Arisaka writes that one of the chants children sang while flying kites played on “tako” (kite) and “tako” (octopus), with words saying that when it comes down you grill it and eat it (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). This poem can be read as based on that chant.
strings.刷った後の検査（出典と仮説の字を読み直す・貼った画像 {0} 枚）: Checks after printing (re-read the source text and the guess text, {0} pasted images)
strings.前から話に聞いていたのは、これなのだなあ、という気持ちを表す言い方。「これがあの: A phrase for the feeling “So this is the one I have heard about!” It is like saying “So this is the famous …!” The old waka poem “Kore ya kono yuku mo kaeru mo …” also begins with these words (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.前の「いぬ」と、この「猿」が、縁語として組み合わされているとも考えられる、と有坂: Arisaka writes that the “inu” (dog) earlier and this “saru” (monkey) may also be paired as related words (engo) (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). In this poem, it can be read as putting the dog and the monkey, which are often named together, at the front and the back.
strings.前の「からくりのちかふも見へて」の意味ははっきりしない、と有坂も書いています（有: Arisaka also writes that the meaning of the earlier part, “karakuri no chikafu mo mihete”, is unclear (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). What the “chikafu” in this poem refers to is not known.
strings.加茂のむかしの車あらそひ: 加茂のむかしの車あらそひ (Kamo no mukashi no kuruma arasohi)
strings.勝ちもしないし、負けもしない、木の人形（木偶の坊）のすもう。勝ち負けは、人の手の: Sumo between wooden dolls (deku no bō) that will neither win nor lose. Winning and losing are in people’s hands. “Sumai” and “sumahi” can be read as plays on both “will not …” and “sumō” (sumo).
strings.十干と十二支の組み合わせの、いちばん目で、はじまりの印として大切にされました。七: The first in the cycle of combinations of the ten jikkan (heavenly stems) and the twelve jūnishi (zodiac animals); it was treasured as a sign of beginnings. Daikokuten, one of the Seven Gods of Good Fortune, has his festival on the day of kinoene (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “kinoene toshi” in this poem can be read as a year of kinoene, which is linked to Daikoku, but that is not certain.
strings.南無あめの鳥: 南無あめの鳥 (namu ame no tori)
strings.口から、知らないうちに流れ出てしまうつばのことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌: Spit that flows out of the mouth without your noticing (from Digital Daijisen). The “yotare” in this poem can be read as “yodare” (drool).
strings.同じ種類のものや、同じくらいのもののことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌の「外: Things of the same kind, or things of the same level (from Digital Daijisen). The “hoka ni takuhi no aranu” in this poem can be read as “with nothing else to match it”.
strings.名前の「うつし」には、伝統の芸の「写し」の心を込めています。: The name “utsushi” carries the spirit of utsushi (写し) in the traditional arts.
strings.品（ひん）のよいおみやげだからと、おもちゃの馬の値段を、とうとう聞く。「ひん」は: Since it is a souvenir of good taste (hin), I finally ask the price of the toy horse. “Hin” can be read as a play on the sound a horse makes. There also seems to be a pun in “tō-tō” (finally), but what it plays on is not known.
strings.四天王のように、手柄を立てられるよう祈っている。山伏のすがたをした子どもたちの、: I pray that they will do great deeds, like the Four Heavenly Kings. I pray for the future of the children dressed as yamabushi (mountain monks).
strings.型紙そのものも直せます。作った人の記録から型紙が直って、次の版になります。: The template itself can be fixed too. Makers’ records improve the template, and it becomes the next version.
strings.型紙のたたき台は、このサイトを作る時に、AI（Claude）が絵と歌から動く仕組: The starting template began as a guess that the AI (Claude) came up with while this site was being built: how the toy might move, based on its picture and poem. The engine turned that guess into the template drawing.
strings.型紙は、AI が考えた ためしの案（仮説）です。切って、折って、組んで、どう工夫: The template is a guess the AI came up with. Cut, fold, and put it together, then write down what you changed in your record; that record is used to make the next template better. In a workshop, you go around this loop once with a facilitator. With utsushi, you can keep going around it on your own afterward.
strings.型紙は正解ではなく、AI が考えた仮説です。作って、動きを確かめて、直していきま: A template is not the right answer. It is a guess the AI came up with. You make it, check how it moves, and improve it.
strings.夏も冬も、赤いふんどし一つで、猿が米をついている。「人に」がどうつながるかは、わ: Summer and winter alike, wearing nothing but a red loincloth, a monkey is pounding rice. How “hito ni” (to people, for people) fits in is not known.
strings.大みそか、人はお金に困って、ぴいぴいと泣いている。代金を取り立てに来た人は、ぶう: On New Year’s Eve, people are short of money and crying “pii-pii”. The bill collector who has come for the money grumbles “bū-bū”.
strings.大山の臼と杵ほど仲のよい、こま（独楽）。もろこしが原で、麦をつく。歌全体が何を言: Tops (koma), as close as the mortar and pestle of Ōyama. On the plain of Morokoshi, they pound barley. What the poem as a whole is saying is not known.
strings.奴凧と同じように、着物の袖がついた形の凧です（精選版 日本国語大辞典より）。この: Like the yakko kite, it is a kite in the shape of a kimono with sleeves (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). In this poem, it can be read as the kite in the picture with the crest of a cross in a circle.
strings.子どもが大きくなっていく、これから先のこと（デジタル大辞泉より）。: The years ahead as a child grows up (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.子どもたちの行く末のこと。端午の節句に子どもが山伏のかっこうをする遊び「山伏学び: The future of the children. The poem is about “Yamabushi Manabi” (playing at being yamabushi), a game in which children dress up as yamabushi at the Boys’ Festival (Tango no Sekku), and these words can be read as celebrating their growth (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.子への思いで迷う親の心を「心の闇」と言い、これは平安時代の藤原兼輔の、親の心は闇: The confusion in a parent’s heart out of love for a child is called “kokoro no yami” (darkness of the heart); this comes from a poem by Fujiwara no Kanesuke of the Heian period, which says that a parent’s heart is not darkness, yet it loses its way on the path of loving a child (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “ko o omofu michi” in this poem can be read as layering a heart that thinks of a child and the road toward Fushimi (whether it is based on Kanesuke’s poem is not certain).
strings.子をおもふみち: 子をおもふみち (ko o omofu michi)
strings.宇津の山ですべって、ころんでしまった。けれども、けがはなかった。腰の下げもの。「: I slipped on Mount Utsu and fell down. But I was not hurt. Things hanging from the waist. “Tawara korohi” can be read as a play on the name of the toy “tawara korobashi” (rolling rice bale). How the last part, “koshi no sagemono” (things hanging from the waist), connects to the words before it is not certain.
strings.家のあとをつぐこと、また、あとをつぐ人のことです（精選版 日本国語大辞典より）。: Carrying on a family line, or the person who carries it on; an heir (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.家の中、または、家族のことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌では、家じゅうの人み: The inside of a house, or a family (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as “everyone in the household”.
strings.山や野にすむ、猫に似たけもののことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌では、人をだ: A cat-like wild animal that lives in the mountains and fields (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as a beast that tricks people.
strings.山寺の夕暮れの鐘を外してしまったのは、花を散らすまいという、茶屋の工夫だろうか。: Was it the teahouse’s clever idea to take down the evening bell of the mountain temple, so as not to scatter the blossoms? (Arisaka Yotarō reads it this way: if the sound of the bell makes the cherry blossoms fall, people will stop coming to see the flowers.)
strings.布のこと。織物を切った小さな切れはしも「きれ」と言います（デジタル大辞泉より）。: Cloth. A small piece cut from woven cloth is also called “kire” (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.年をとって、体の力や気持ちの張りが弱っていくことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この: Growing old and losing bodily strength and spirit (from Digital Daijisen). The “oikomi nureba” in this poem can be read as “once he has grown old and weak”.
strings.張子で作った、首が動く虎の玩具。強そうに見えて実は弱い物のたとえにも使われます（: A papier-mâché tiger toy whose head moves. It is also used for something that looks strong but is actually weak (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). Like the papier-mâché dog, it was displayed to ward off evil (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.強い武者たちの中で、ひときわ目立つ二つの頭。赤いのは平家、白いのは源氏。: Among the mighty warriors, two heads stand out. The red one is the Heike (Taira clan), and the white one is the Genji (Minamoto clan).
strings.御来迎と首振り虎の型紙は、コンピューターの中の {0}D で折って組み立て、紙ど: For the Goraigo and papier-mâché tiger templates, the engine folds and assembles the paper in {0}D inside the computer. It checks on its own that no pieces of paper bump into each other and that the colored sides face outward (places where pieces might bump are written down for people to look at). The assembly is also shown in step-by-step pictures and a short video.
strings.御来迎を拝むにつけても、怠けずにいよう。朝に夕に、南無あめの鳥。: Whenever I worship the Goraigo, I will not slacken. Morning and evening: namu ame no tori.
strings.思っていたより早く、もうそうなった、と感じるときに使う言葉で、「はやくも」「もは: A word used when you feel that something has already happened sooner than you expected; it is close in meaning to “hayaku mo” (so soon) and “mohaya” (by now) (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as “today, already”.
strings.怠けないでいよう。「怠る」に、「…まい」と心に決める意味の「じ」が付いた形（デジ: I will not slacken. It is “okotaru” (to neglect, to slacken) with “ji”, which means resolving “I will not …” (from Digital Daijisen). What is not to be neglected is not known.
strings.恋しい気持ちや、人をねたむ気持ちが、胸の中で熱く燃えるようすを、火にたとえた言い: A phrase that compares feelings of love or jealousy burning hot in the heart to a fire (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it goes on to say that this fire is “kakure” (hidden).
strings.恋しく思っても、とても届かない。羽子板は雲の上の高いお方、わたし（羽根）は身分の: Though I long for you, I can never reach you. The battledore (hagoita) is a noble one high above the clouds, and I (the shuttlecock) am of low birth.
strings.戦いに勝って、自分たちの陣にもどることです。「凱旋（がいせん）」と同じような意味: To return to one’s own camp after winning a battle; it means about the same as “gaisen” (a triumphant return) (from Digital Daijisen). The furigana characters (such as whether there are voicing marks) are not certain.
strings.手がら。りっぱな働き（精選版 日本国語大辞典より）。: An achievement; a splendid deed (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.手ぬぐいなどで、頭からほおを包むようにかぶること（デジタル大辞泉より）。: Wearing a hand towel or similar cloth over the head so that it wraps around the cheeks (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.手のひらのことで、また、自分の力のとどく所という意味にも使います（デジタル大辞泉: The palm of the hand; it is also used to mean the area your power can reach (from Digital Daijisen). The “hito no te no uchi ni ari” in this poem can be read as “winning and losing depend on people”.
strings.手を使って、こまかな物をこしらえること。こしらえた物のことも言います（デジタル大: Making small, detailed things by hand. It also means the things made this way (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.拝むにつけて: 拝むにつけて (ogamu ni tsukete)
strings.拝むのにあわせて。拝む時にも（「…につけて」の意味。デジタル大辞泉より）。: Along with worshipping; also when worshipping (the meaning of “… ni tsukete”, from Digital Daijisen).
strings.振り鼓（ふりつづみ）。もとは舞楽で使う楽器で、その形をまねたおもちゃです。でんで: A swing drum (furitsuzumi). It was first an instrument used in bugaku court dance, and the toy copies its shape. It belongs to the same family as the den-den drum (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.描く前の検査（寸法の範囲・印字域・重なり・玩具ごとの動きの計算）: Checks before drawing (range of dimensions, printable area, overlaps, each toy’s motion calculation)
strings.旅や出かけた先から持って帰ったり、人の家へ持っていったりする品物のことです（精選: Things you bring home from a trip or a place you went to, or take to someone’s house (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “miyakemono” in this poem can be read as “miyagemono” (a souvenir).
strings.昔、日本で中国のことを呼んだ名前です（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌では、「こま（: The name by which people in Japan called China long ago (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as setting two old names of countries side by side: “Koma” (高麗) and “Morokoshi”.
strings.昔からの言い伝えで、月の中に住んでいるといわれるうさぎ（精選版 日本国語大辞典よ: A rabbit that, according to an old legend, lives on the moon (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.昔のこよみの五月のことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌では、五月五日の端午の節: The fifth month of the old calendar (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as the time of the Boys’ Festival (Tango no Sekku) on the fifth day of the fifth month.
strings.昔のこよみ（陰暦）の六月を、別の名で呼んだ言い方です（デジタル大辞泉より）。: Another name for the sixth month of the old (lunar) calendar (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.昔の国の名前で、今の東京都・埼玉県と、神奈川県の東のほうにあたります（デジタル大: The name of an old province, covering what is now Tokyo, Saitama Prefecture, and the eastern part of Kanagawa Prefecture (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.昔の言葉「をかし」の形で、心がひかれておもしろい、という意味。狂歌のような人を笑: A form of the old word “okashi” (をかし), meaning charming and interesting. In poems meant to make people laugh, such as kyōka (comic poems), it was often used to mean comical or funny (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.昔の言葉で、顔かたちの美しくない女の人のこと。「美人」と反対の言葉です（精選版: In old Japanese, a woman whose looks are not beautiful. It is the opposite of “bijin” (a beautiful woman) (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.昔は「うそふく」とも書いた「うそぶく」の事。虎などがほえる、という意味と、強がり: “Usobuku”, which was once also written “usofuku”. It can mean that a tiger or another beast roars, or that someone talks big (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). Which meaning this poem uses is not known.
strings.月のいちばんはじめの日を「ついたち」と言い、市が開かれることを「市が立つ」と言い: The first day of a month is called “tsuitachi”, and holding a market is called “ichi ga tatsu” (a market stands) (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “tsuitatsu ichi” in this poem can be read as a market held on the first day of the month, but that is not certain.
strings.月のうさぎや、魚や亀のすむ広い海の上を、すずめのように飛びはねる、はねむし。「ひ: Over the wide sea where the moon rabbit, fish, and turtles live, the hanemushi (hopping bug) leaps and hops like a sparrow. The meaning of “hinzu” is not clearly known.
strings.有坂の本ではこの所が「飛んづ」と書かれ、続く「はね」と合わせて、すずめのように「: In Arisaka’s book, this part is written with the kanji for “fly” (飛んづ), and together with the “hane” that follows, he reads it as “tobihaneru”: to leap and hop like a sparrow (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). What the word “hinzu” itself means is not known.
strings.有坂は、からくり人形の奴と、「酒に廻され」の独楽とを結び付けた歌だと解いています: Arisaka explains it as a poem that ties the karakuri yakko doll to the top through “sake ni mawasare” (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). In this poem, being made drunk by sake and the top in the picture can be read as layered through the word “mawasu” (to turn, to spin).
strings.有坂は、この市は富士神社の山開きのことで、その日にかぎって唐団扇と麦わらの蛇を売: Arisaka writes that this market was the opening of the climbing season at the Fuji Shrine, and that only on that day, Chinese-style fans (tōuchiwa) and wheat-straw snakes were sold (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). The “uchiwa” in this poem can be read as these Chinese-style fans.
strings.有坂は、この歌は、木の人形はよいこともしないし悪いこともしない、ということわざの: Arisaka writes that this poem takes the meaning of a saying, that a wooden doll does neither good nor bad, and plays it on sumo (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). The “make mo sumahi” in this poem can be read two ways: “will not lose either” and “sumahi” (sumo).
strings.有坂は、この歌は、東海道の宇津の山の名物だった十団子と、俵ころばしと、腰の下げも: Arisaka writes that this poem works in three toys: the tōdango (ten dumplings), a famous product of Mount Utsu on the Tōkaidō road, the tawara korobashi, and things hung from the waist (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). In this poem, the mountain’s name “Utsu no yama” can be read as calling to mind its famous tōdango.
strings.有坂は、この歌を、江戸の牛込にある赤城神社にちなんで作られた歌として読んでいます: Arisaka reads this poem as one made in connection with the Akagi Shrine in Ushigome, Edo (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). The “Akagi” in the poem (赤木) can be read as this Akagi (赤城).
strings.有坂は、竹馬を見て、おさない頃を思い出すことが、この歌の意味だと書いています（有: Arisaka writes that the meaning of this poem is that seeing a bamboo horse reminds you of when you were little (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). The “oi no kokoro” in this poem can be read as the heart of an old person.
strings.有坂は、終わりの「にごりぬる」は、絵の徳利を利かせた（結び付けた）言葉だ、と書い: Arisaka writes that the last part, “nigorinuru” (has become muddy), is a word that ties in the sake bottle in the picture (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). In this poem, it can be read as the tobi’s cry sounding muddy, not clear, but how it ties in with the sake bottle is not known.
strings.有坂は、袖凧も鳶凧も紙なので、干したたこのように焼いて食べることはできない、とい: Arisaka says the meaning of this poem is that both the sleeve kite and the tobi kite are paper, so you cannot grill and eat them like dried octopus. He writes that even if you take “kaminari” as “thunder”, it only means the kite with thunder painted on it (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). The “kaminari” in this poem can be read as layering “kami nari” (it is paper) and the thunder kite in the picture.
strings.有坂は、赤い髪の猩々は、中国から伝わった考えで、豊かさと長生きを表すとします。そ: Arisaka says that the red-haired shōjō is an idea that came from China and stands for wealth and long life. So he writes that this poem can be read simply as saying that the doll seller who spread shōjō toys far and wide gradually became rich (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). The fun of this poem can be read as this: because he sold lucky shōjō, something lucky happened to the doll seller too.
strings.有坂は「松坂こへてかしまはじまる」を、寛永のころから江戸ではやった鹿島踊のことだ: Arisaka writes that “Matsuzaka kohete Kashima hajimaru” is about the Kashima dance (Kashima odori), which was popular in Edo from around the Kan’ei era, and that the Kashima dance was danced while singing “Matsuzaka koete” (crossing Matsuzaka) (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). The “kohete” in this poem can be read as “koete” (crossing).
strings.有坂は「湯殿の大踊」を、湯殿山で「松の聖」と呼ばれる神楽が、まわりを気にせず、に: Arisaka writes that “Yudono no ō-odori” is the kagura (sacred dance) called “Matsu no Hijiri” at Mount Yudono, dancing around merrily without caring about anything around it (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). In this poem, it can be read as saying that the playing ended up as such a big dance.
strings.朝な夕な: 朝な夕な (asa na yū na)
strings.朝に夕に。いつも（デジタル大辞泉より）。: In the morning and in the evening; always (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.本物そっくりに、よく似せた鶏の作り物。そそっかしい人は、本物だと思ってしまうだろ: A model chicken, made to look just like a real one. A careless person would probably think it is real.
strings.束ねる（名前・連絡先は入れない）: Gather them (no names or contact details)
strings.東京の芝大神宮（芝神明）で、毎年九月のお祭りの間に開かれる、しょうがを売る市です: A market selling ginger, held every year during the September festival at Shiba Daijingū (Shiba Shinmei) shrine in Tokyo (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.松の木に吹きつける風のことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌では、次の「こと（琴: Wind blowing against pine trees (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as linked with the next word, “koto” (a stringed instrument), as an image of the pine wind blowing as if playing a koto, but that is not certain.
strings.松ぼっくり（松かさ）のこと。松の木の実で、昔は「まつふぐり」とも呼びました（精選: A pine cone (matsubokkuri, also called matsukasa). It is the fruit of the pine tree, and long ago it was also called “matsufuguri” (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten).
strings.桃から生まれた男の子が主人公の昔話です。お供の犬・猿・きじと鬼が島へ行き、鬼を退: A folktale whose hero is a boy born from a peach. With his companions, a dog, a monkey, and a pheasant, he goes to Onigashima (Ogre Island), defeats the ogres, and brings back treasure (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.桃太郎が鬼が島から勝って帰る日には、わんわん（犬）も、りっぱな晴れ着にくらいつい: On the day Momotarō comes home victorious from Onigashima, even the bow-wow (the dog) clung to his fine festive clothes, or so it can be read (the meaning of “kuraitsukinuru” is not certain).
strings.今は、作った人の記録を Claude に渡して、次の型紙の案を作っています。どの: For now, we hand the records of the people who made the toys to Claude, and Claude drafts the next template. People decide which version to use.
strings.次の版は、今のたたき台の型紙にだけ足せます。: The next version can only be added to the current starting template.
strings.うずくまった丸い形は、転がりにくい底の広いダルマと同じで、台に置けば重さの真ん中: A crouching round shape is like a daruma with a wide base that does not roll easily: if you set it on a stand, the middle of its weight (the center of gravity) is low, and it comes back when pushed. If the guess is that it floats on water, it is like a bath toy: a light, hollow shell floats because the water it pushes aside pushes it back up.
strings.うまくいかなかった所と、どう工夫したか（あれば）: What did not go well, and what you changed (if anything)
strings.うまく表示できませんでした。少し待って、もう一度開いてください。: Could not be shown properly. Wait a moment, then open it again.

strings.かざぐるまが回るのは、ひねった羽が風を横へそらし、そのお返しに羽が横へ押されるか: A pinwheel turns because the twisted blades push the wind to the side, and in return the blades are pushed to the side. It is like using the blades of an electric fan the other way around. The guess that the blades are folded into little cups is like the cups of an anemometer or the buckets of a water wheel: the open side is pushed harder, so it turns.

strings.ここでは、おもちゃを選ぶと、すぐに紙の型紙を作れます。紙と糸で作って、動くかたし: Here, pick a toy and you can print its paper template right away. Make it with paper and string, and check whether it moves. The template is not the right answer. It is a guess the AI came up with: “Maybe it works like this?” The paper answers first. When it does not move, that is also one of the paper’s answers. Write down what you changed. That helps make the next template better. After you write your own thoughts, you can get a reply from the AI (Claude), too. A paper model that moves does not prove how the original was made. It is not an exact copy of the old toy. It is for trying things out.
strings.ここで言うおもちゃは、手で動かしてたしかめられる形（トイ＝モデル）のことです。買: By “toy” we mean a model you can move with your hands to find out how it works (toy = model). It is not a finished product someone buys for you, and it is not an exact copy of the real thing.

strings.これも何の作り物かはわからないので、置き方の仕組みでたとえます。台なしで置かれた: We do not know what this one is meant to be either, so we compare it by how it sits. A long, thin thing placed without a stand stays put without rolling. It is like an eraser on a desk or a stone with a flat-cut bottom: the wider the bottom, the steadier it is. If the guess is that it floats on water, it is like a boat floating in the bath.
strings.しなり: 柄に貼る長さが短いと、振った時に付け根の紙が曲がる。長く貼ると棒ごと動: Bending: If the part glued to the handle is short, the paper at the base bends when you wave it. If you glue a longer part, the whole stick moves.

strings.しなり: 竹串を貼った長さが短いと、振った時に紙の付け根が先に曲がる: Bending: If the part where the bamboo skewer is glued is short, the base of the paper bends first when you wave it.

strings.しなり: 細い棒に広い紙を付けて振ると、空気に押されて紙がしなる。貼る長さを長く: Bending: If you wave wide paper on a thin stick, the air pushes on the paper and it bends. If you glue a longer part of it to the stick, it bends less.
strings.しなり: 細い棒の先に紙を付けて振ると、紙は空気に押されてしなる。貼る長さを長く: Bending: If you wave paper on the tip of a thin stick, the air pushes the paper and it bends. The longer the glued length, the less it bends.

strings.すき間と摩擦: 切れ目が狭いと紙どうしがこすれて止まり、広いとぐらつく: Gaps and friction: If the slit is narrow, the paper rubs and gets stuck. If it is wide, it wobbles.

strings.ずんぐりした鳥の形は、底が広くて重さの真ん中（重心）が低いので、置物として倒れに: A chubby bird shape has a wide bottom, and the middle of its weight (the center of gravity) is low, so as an ornament it does not tip over easily. If we read it as papier-mâché, it is a light shell of layered, glued paper that keeps its shape even though it is empty inside, just like an eggshell or a piñata.

strings.てこ: 支点から遠い所ほど大きく動く。腰が支点なら、頭と杵の先が一番大きく振れる: Lever: The farther from the pivot, the more it moves. If the waist is the pivot, the head and the tip of the pestle swing the most.
strings.てこ: 支点（軸）から押す所が近いほど、動かす側は大きく動く。力は小さくてよいが: Lever: The closer the spot you push is to the pivot (axis), the more the moving side moves. The force can be small, but the distance moved is large.
strings.てこ: 袖が軸の近くで回るなら、糸を少し引くだけで袖の先は大きく上がる: Lever: If the sleeve turns near the pivot, pulling the string only a little raises the tip of the sleeve a lot.
strings.てこ: 軸の近くを少し動かすと、軸から遠い所は大きく動く。力は小さく、動きは大き: Lever: If you move a little near the axle, the part far from the axle moves a lot. The force is small, and the movement is big.
strings.てこ: 軸（支点）から遠い所ほど、同じ動きでも大きく振れる。はさみの刃の先と持ち: Lever: The farther a spot is from the pivot, the more it swings for the same push. Think of the tips of scissor blades and the handles.
strings.てこ: 軸（支点）の近くを少し動かすと、軸から遠い袖の先は大きく振れる: Lever: Move a spot near the pivot (fulcrum) a little, and the tips of the sleeves, far from the pivot, swing a lot.
strings.てこ: 軸（支点）の近くを少し動かすと、遠い所は大きく動く。くちばしの先が大きく: Lever: If you move a spot near the pivot (fulcrum) a little, a spot far away moves a lot. This is why the tip of the beak swings a lot.
strings.てこ: 軸（支点）の近くを少し引くと、軸から遠い所は大きく動く: Lever: Pull a little near the pivot (fulcrum), and the parts far from the pivot move a lot.
strings.てこ: 軸（支点）の近くを少し引くと、軸から遠い頭の先は大きく動く: Lever: Pull a little near the pivot (fulcrum), and the tip of the head, far from the pivot, moves a lot.
strings.てこと柄: 長い柄は小さな力で持ち上げられるが、先が重いと手元で支える力が要る: Lever and handle: A long handle can be lifted with little force, but if the end is heavy, your hand has to work harder to hold it up.

strings.歌全体がねたみを表していて、この句は、能の『鉄輪』の、車の輪がめぐるように、つら: Arisaka writes that the whole poem expresses jealousy, and that this line is probably based on a passage in the noh play Kanawa, a bitter passage saying that, as a cart wheel turns, the one who caused pain will in turn be paid back (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). This poem can be read as linking the story of the fire in the heart to the old story of the quarrel at Kamo.
strings.武士の家でいちばんの宝は、あとをつぐ男の子と、弓矢なのだなあ。: So the greatest treasures of a samurai house are the boy who will carry on the family, and the bow and arrows!
strings.武蔵の国の赤木の、や戸にいる山猫は、けものなので、人をだましてまよわせるのだ。「: The wildcat at the “yato” of Akagi in the province of Musashi is a beast, so it tricks people and leads them astray. What “yato” refers to is not known.
strings.毛の生えていない、チョウやガの子どもの虫。俳句では、秋の季節を表す言葉です（デジ: A caterpillar with no hair: the young of a butterfly or moth. In haiku, it is a word for autumn (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.歌舞伎で、恋の場面の役が得意な役者のこと。恋の上手な男の人のことも言います（デジ: In kabuki, an actor who is good at playing love scenes. It also means a man who is good at love (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.武器のことも言いますが、ここでは、勇ましく強い武者のことと読むのがよい、と有坂は: It can also mean weapons, but Arisaka writes that here it is best read as brave, strong warriors (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.水無月（昔のこよみの六月）の一日に立つ市の売り物は、ほかに並ぶ物のない、うちわだ: What is sold at the market held on the first day of Minazuki (the sixth month of the old calendar) is fans, with nothing else to match them! The “jiya” at the end can be read as also playing on “ja” (snake). The phrase “tsuitatsu ichi” is not certain.
strings.江戸で人気を集めた浄瑠璃（人形芝居で物語を語る芸）の語り手で、のちに桜井丹波少掾: A jōruri chanter who became popular in Edo (jōruri is the art of telling the story in a puppet play). He later took the name Sakurai Tanba no Shōjō. He started “Kinpira-bushi”, a style of chanting in which the strong hero Kinpira does great deeds (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.江戸時代、武士の家に仕え、槍や挟み箱を手にして、行列の先頭に立った人のことです（: In the Edo period, a man who served a samurai household and walked at the front of a procession carrying a spear or a lidded box (hasamibako) (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as also meaning the “karakuri yakko” doll in the picture.
strings.江戸時代、疱瘡（ほうそう）という病気が治った子どもに、お酒をまぜたお湯をかけたこ: In the Edo period, pouring hot water mixed with sake over a child who had recovered from an illness called hōsō (smallpox), or that water itself. It is also said that bamboo-grass leaves were dipped in the water and used to sprinkle it (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as saying that even the bath after the illness is over, and a stage has come to an end.
strings.物を売って、世の中のすみずみまで行きわたらせることです（精選版 日本国語大辞典よ: Selling things so that they spread to every corner of the world (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). In this poem, it can be read as the doll seller selling shōjō dolls far and wide.
strings.独楽もしんぼう: 独楽もしんぼう (koma mo shinbō)
strings.猿に似た想像上の生き物で、赤く長い毛と人のような顔を持ち、お酒が好きだといわれま: An imaginary creature like a monkey, with long red hair and a human-like face, said to love sake. In the noh play Shōjō, Kōfū, a son who takes good care of his parents, sells sake and gradually becomes rich (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The end of the poem, “shidai-shidai ni fūki nari keri” (gradually became rich), may be based on this noh story, but that is not certain.
strings.猿も、五月には木を替えて竹にのぼる。風車のほうは、おりているのだ。「おりて」が何: In the fifth month, even the monkey changes trees and climbs bamboo. As for the pinwheel, it has come down. What “orite” (coming down) means is not known.
strings.王さまの政治がよいので、だれも太鼓を打つ必要がなく、こけが深く生えている、という: Because the king rules well, no one needs to beat the drum, so moss grows thick on it. It is a way of saying that the country is peaceful and well governed (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.生姜市で、「ちぎ」も「ふた見」も聞くと、伊勢のようだと人は言う。「ふた見」が何を: At the Ginger Market, when people hear both “chigi” and “futami”, they say it is just like Ise. What “futami” refers to is not known.
strings.田や畑で作物を育てる人。農家の人のことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。: A person who grows crops in rice paddies and fields; a farmer (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.百姓と奴が着ている物をよく見ると、松ぼっくりでございます。: If you look closely at what the farmer and the yakko (a samurai’s servant) are wearing, it is pine cones, if you please.
strings.石橋の獅子のような、強く勇ましい獣も、牡丹の花のもとでは、尺八ほどの長いよだれを: Even a strong, brave beast like the lion of Shakkyō must let its drool hang down under the peony flowers, as long as a shakuhachi flute (that this is while it sleeps under the peonies is Arisaka’s reading).
strings.神さまや仏さまに特に関わりのある日で、その日にお参りすると、いつもより多くのご利: A day with a special tie to a particular god or Buddha; visiting on that day is believed to bring more blessings than usual. For example, day {0} of each month is Kannon’s day, and day {1} is Fudō’s day (from Digital Daijisen). The poem can also be read on as “the fair day of the dog” (inu), but which god’s or Buddha’s fair day it is, is not known.
strings.神さまや仏さまの力が宿っていて、持つ人を守ってくれるという小さな品やお札、つまり: A small item or paper charm that holds the power of a god or Buddha and protects the person who carries it; in other words, an omamori (amulet) (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). What kind of charm the “tsutsumamori” in this poem is, is not known.
strings.神主のすがたで神のお告げを伝えて回った人たちの太鼓を、小さくしたおもちゃも「鹿島: A toy that was a small version of the drum carried by people who went around dressed as Shinto priests, telling people the words of the gods, was also called “Kashima odori”. Originally, it is the name of a dance said to have come from faith in Kashima Shrine in Ibaraki Prefecture (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “Kashima” in this poem can be read as this Kashima dance, linked to the toy drum in the picture.
strings.神奈川県の中ほどにある山で、山の上には、雨ごいの神さまをまつる阿夫利神社がありま: A mountain in central Kanagawa Prefecture. At the top is the Afuri Shrine, which honors a god people pray to for rain (from Digital Daijisen). The “Ōyama no” in this poem can be read as meaning handmade souvenirs from Ōyama.
strings.神社の屋根の上で交わっている木を「千木（ちぎ）」と言い、お祭りで売られた箱は「千: The crossed beams on top of a shrine roof are called “chigi” (千木), and the boxes sold at the festival are called “chigibako” (千木箱) (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “chigi” in this poem can be read as a short name for those chigibako.
strings.穀物を粉にしたり、白くしたりするほか、おもちをつくのにも使う道具です（デジタル大: A tool used to grind grain into flour or to polish it white, and also to pound mochi (rice cakes) (from Digital Daijisen).
strings.空の高いところ、遠くはなれたところ、また、宮中（天皇の住まい）のことです（デジタ: A high place in the sky, a far-off place, or the imperial court (where the emperor lives) (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as standing for a high rank that is out of reach.
strings.立っていられなくなって、倒れることです（デジタル大辞泉より）。この歌では、人にも: To be unable to stay standing and fall over (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as a word used for both people and tops.
strings.竹でできた、たてに持って吹く笛で、長さ一尺八寸（約 {0} センチ）がもとになる: A bamboo flute held upright and blown; its basic length is one shaku and eight sun (about {0} centimeters) (from Digital Daijisen). The “shakuhachi hoto no” in this poem means “shakuhachi hodo no” (as long as a shakuhachi), and can be read as an exaggerated way of saying the drool is about as long as a shakuhachi.
strings.竹馬を見ると、年をとった人の心も、おさない子どもにかえる。これで（この絵本は）お: Seeing a bamboo horse (takeuma), even the heart of an old person goes back to being a small child. With this, (this picture book) is complete to the end: a joyful nobori (banner). What the “gusa” in “osanagusa” means is not certain.
strings.米やいも、炭などを入れておく、わらを編んだ袋のことです（デジタル大辞泉より）。こ: A bag woven of straw, for holding rice, potatoes, charcoal, and so on (from Digital Daijisen). In this poem, it can be read as the rice bale of the toy “tawara korobashi”.
strings.絵に描かれた屏風の玩具の名前で、団十郎など役者の紋が描かれ、「団十郎のからくり屏: Arisaka writes that it is the name of the folding-screen toy in the picture, which had the crests of actors such as Danjūrō painted on it and was also called “Danjūrō’s karakuri screen” (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). In this poem, it can be read as layering the heart’s fire being “kakure” (hidden) with this name.
strings.羽子板の表に、宮中で行われた左義長という行事の古い様子が描かれているので、羽子板: Arisaka writes that the battledore was called “Kumoi no kimi” (the noble one above the clouds) because its front shows an old scene of sagichō, an event held at the imperial court (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}).
strings.羽根が、自分のことを身分の低い者だとへりくだって言った言葉だ、と有坂は読んでいま: Arisaka reads it as the shuttlecock humbly calling itself a person of low rank (from Arisaka Yotarō, Nihon Gangushi, Part 2, p. {0}). In this poem, the height of “kumoi” and the lowness of “shizu” can be read as set against each other.
strings.老いのこゝろ: 老いのこゝろ (oi no kokoro)
strings.胸がどきどきする、と下戸（お酒の飲めない人）はいやがる。後ろの「酒の中へ ひとつ: The geko (a person who cannot drink sake) does not like it, saying, “It makes my heart pound.” What the rest of the poem, “sake no naka e hitotsu naru tote suzu ya idenuran” (into the sake, saying “one …”, has a bell come out?), is saying is not known.
strings.胸の中に隠していた火（恋しさや、ねたむ心）も、かくれ屏風も、とうとう表に出てしま: The fire hidden in my heart (longing and jealousy), and the kakure byōbu (hiding screen) too, have finally come out into the open, like the carriage quarrel at Kamo long ago.

In the story, when a monk comes to a stone bridge on Mount Seiryō (Qingliang) in China, a lion appears and dances bravely among the blooming peonies (from Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten). The “Shakkyō no takeki kemono” (the fierce beast of Shakkyō) in this poem can be read as the lion in this noh play.
strings.腰にさげて持ち歩く物をまとめて呼ぶ名で、印籠や巾着などがそうです（デジタル大辞泉: A name for all the things carried hanging from the waist, such as inrō (small cases) and kinchaku (drawstring pouches) (from Digital Daijisen). The “koshi no sagemono” in this poem can be read as these “sagemono”.

The guess that it leans against a support is the same idea as the support at the back of a photo frame.

strings.振り子: 吊った物を揺らすと、戻る力で行ったり来たりする。糸が長いほどゆっくり: Pendulum: If you swing a hanging thing, it goes back and forth because of the force that pulls it back. The longer the string, the slower it swings.
strings.振り子: 戻る力があると行き過ぎて反対へ揺れ、だんだん小さくなって止まる（空気と: Pendulum: With a force that pulls it back, it swings past the middle to the other side, gets smaller and smaller, and stops (because of the air and the rubbing at the axis).
strings.振り子: 揺れは行ったり来たりしてだんだん小さくなる。軸のこすれが大きいとすぐ止: Pendulum: The swing goes back and forth and gets smaller and smaller. If there is a lot of rubbing at the axis, it stops quickly.
strings.振り子の速さ: 重心が軸から遠いほど、揺れはゆっくり。近いほど小刻みに揺れる: Pendulum speed: The farther the center of gravity is from the axis, the slower the swing. The closer it is, the quicker and smaller the swings.

strings.掲げる物: 旗や幟のように、棒の先に付けて高く見せる物は、風を受けると棒がしなる: Things held up high: Things fixed to the end of a stick to show them high up, like flags and banners, make the stick bend when they catch the wind.
strings.揺らして鳴る: 中に玉があれば、打たなくても揺らすだけで壁に当たって鳴る: Sound from rocking: If there are balls inside, they hit the wall and sound just by rocking it, without hitting it.
strings.揺れの続き: 軸でこすれる力が小さいほど、揺れが長く続く: How long it keeps swinging: The less the rubbing force at the axle, the longer the swinging lasts.
strings.揺れの速さ: 重りを軸から遠くすると、揺れはゆっくりになる（長い振り子ほどゆっく: Swinging speed: If you put the weight farther from the axis, the swing gets slower (a longer pendulum swings more slowly).
strings.摩擦: 先がとがっていると床とこすれる所が小さく、勢いが減りにくい: Friction: If the tip is pointed, the part that rubs the floor is small, and the energy does not drop as fast.
strings.摩擦: 差した矢が止まるのは紙どうしがこすれる力。きつすぎると抜けない: Friction: An arrow stays in place because the pieces of paper rub against each other. If it is too tight, it will not come out.
strings.摩擦: 床と芯の先がこすれると回りが弱まる。つるつるの床ほど長く回る: Friction: When the tip of the core rubs on the floor, the spinning gets weaker. The smoother the floor, the longer it spins.
strings.摩擦: 矢が袋の中で止まるのは、紙どうしがこすれる力。きつすぎると抜けない: Friction: An arrow stays in the bag because of the force of paper rubbing on paper. If it is too tight, it will not come out.
strings.摩擦: 筒の中で紙どうしがこすれると、戻る力の一部がそこで使われて、途中で止まる: Friction: when paper rubs against paper inside the tube, part of the springing-back force is used up there, and it stops halfway.
strings.摩擦: 軸の穴がきつすぎると動きが鈍く、ゆるすぎるとぐらつく。竹串を通す穴の大き: Friction: If the hole for the pivot is too tight, it moves stiffly. If it is too loose, it wobbles. It changes with the size of the hole the bamboo skewer goes through.
strings.支え: 後ろに足を開くと、底の面が三角に広がる（写真立て・イーゼルと同じ）: Support: If you open a leg at the back, the bottom surface spreads into a triangle (the same as a photo frame or an easel).
strings.支えの角度: 立てかける支えは、開く角度が大きいほど倒れにくいが、場所を取る: Angle of the support: The wider the support opens, the harder it is to knock over, but it takes up more room.
strings.支える面: {0} 本の足の先を結んだ四角。細長い四角は、短い辺の向きに倒れやす: Supporting area: The four-sided shape made by joining the tips of the {0} legs. A long, thin four-sided shape tips easily in the direction of its short side.
strings.支える面: 丸い底でも、台に触れる所が広ければ倒れにくい: Supporting area: Even with a round bottom, it is harder to tip if the part touching the base is wide.
strings.支える面: 台が広いほど、倒れるまでに大きく傾けられる。甲羅の低い亀は重心も低い: Supporting area: The wider the base, the more you can tilt it before it falls. A turtle with a low shell also has a low center of gravity.
strings.支える面: 台と、立てかけた時の支えの足元が作る三角形。広いほど倒れにくい: Supporting area: The triangle made by the base and the foot of the support when it leans. The wider it is, the harder it is to tip.
strings.支える面: 底が丸いと台に触れる所が狭い。紙の台を付けると面が広がる: Supporting area: If the bottom is round, only a small spot touches the stand. Adding a paper base makes the area wider.
strings.支える面: 底の広さ。しぼった口が上にあると、上は軽くて細い形になる: Supporting area: How wide the bottom is. With the tightened mouth at the top, the upper part becomes light and narrow.
strings.支える面: 底の広さ。首が細くても、底が広ければ安定する: Supporting area: The width of the bottom. Even with a thin neck, it is steady if the bottom is wide.
strings.支える面: 脚の底の広さ。脚を広げるほど倒れにくい（三脚やグラスの足と同じ）: Supporting area: The width of the bottom of the foot. The wider you spread the foot, the harder it is to tip (the same as a tripod or the foot of a glass).
strings.支える面: 足や台が作る面が広いほど倒れにくい。{0} 本足の亀は面が広い: Supporting area: The wider the area made by the legs or the base, the harder it is to tip. A turtle with {0} legs has a wide area.
strings.支える面: 足や台の縁を結んだ形。この面の外に重心が出ると倒れる: Supporting area: The shape you get by joining the edges of the feet or the base. If the center of gravity goes outside this area, it falls over.
strings.支える面: 足や台の縁を結んだ形。胴が長い犬は前後の足の間が広く、前後には倒れに: Supporting area: The shape you get by joining the edges of the feet or the base. A dog with a long body has a wide gap between its front and back legs, so it does not tip forward or backward easily.
strings.支える面: 鍋の底が台に触れる広さ。平らな底ほど安定する: Supporting area: How much of the bottom of the pot touches the stand. A flatter bottom is more stable.

strings.棒の先に貼った行灯は、旗や、お祭りの提灯の竿と同じで、振ると棒より先に紙がしなり: A lantern stuck on the end of a stick is like a flag or the pole of a festival lantern: when you swing it, the paper bends before the stick does. Another guess is that it hangs on a string. That is like a hanging wind chime or a mobile: it turns until the middle of its weight (the center of gravity) is right below the string.
strings.棒の先に首を貼って振る仮説は、ペープサート（紙の人形劇）や、運動会の旗と同じで、: One guess is that a head is stuck on the end of a stick and waved. That is like paper stick puppets or a flag at a sports day: when you wave it, the paper bends before the stick does. Another guess is that the head hangs on an axis and swings. That is like a nodding doll or a yajirobe (balancing toy): when the middle of its weight (the center of gravity) is below the axis, it swings back even after you tilt it.
strings.棒の先に鳥を付けてかざすのは、旗や風車を棒の先に付けて走るのと同じで、棒を貼った: Holding up a bird on a stick is the same as running with a flag or pinwheel on a stick: if the part where the stick is glued is short, the paper bends first. Another guess is that it hangs from a pivot and swings. That is like a swing in the park or a balancing toy (yajirobe) on your finger. The center of gravity is below the pivot, so it swings back when you tilt it.
strings.棒の先の獅子頭を振る仮説は、旗を振るのと同じで、柄が短いと紙の方が先にしなります: One guess is that you wave a lion head on the end of a stick. That is like waving a flag: if the handle is short, the paper bends first. Another guess is that the jaw moves with a string. That is like a flapping-mouth puppet (a ventriloquist’s puppet): the weight of the jaw opens the mouth, and pulling the string closes it.
strings.棒の先の馬の頭を持って走るまねをする仮説は、棒馬（ホビーホース）と同じ遊びです。: One guess is that you hold a horse head on the end of a stick and pretend to run. That is the same play as a hobby horse. Another guess is that the head hangs on an axle and swings. That is like a yajirobe: the head nods with every bounce. A third guess is that a wheel is put on the end. That is like a toy car you push along.
strings.棒の先の鳥を振る仮説は、手持ちの風車やペロペロキャンディを振るのと同じで、柄が短: One guess is that you wave a bird on the end of a stick. That is like waving a hand-held pinwheel or a swirl lollipop: if the handle is short, the base of the paper bends first. Another guess is that it hangs on an axle and swings. That is like a yajirobe (a balancing toy) or a hanging decoration that swings gently (a mobile).
